claim: Functional magnetic resonance imaging using blood oxygenation level dependent (BOLD) contrast is well established as one of the most powerful methods for mapping human brain function.
source: Functional magnetic resonance imaging using blood oxygenation level dependent (BOLD) contrast is well established as one of the most powerful methods for mapping human brain function.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific consensus in the field of neuroimaging.

claim: Numerous studies have measured how low-frequency BOLD signal fluctuations from the brain are correlated between voxels in a resting state.
source: Numerous studies have measured how low-frequency BOLD signal fluctuations from the brain are correlated between voxels in a resting state, and have exploited these signals to infer functional connectivity within specific neural circuits.
evidence: This refers to the body of existing literature on resting state fMRI in the brain.

claim: There have been no previous substantiated reports of resting state correlations in the spinal cord prior to this study.
source: However, to date there have been no previous substantiated reports of resting state correlations in the spinal cord.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature, supported by the discussion of Wei et al. (2010) having equivocal results.

claim: Robust functional connectivity was observed between left and right ventral (motor) horns in healthy volunteers.
source: In a cohort of healthy volunteers, we observed robust functional connectivity between left and right ventral (motor) horns, and between left and right dorsal (sensory) horns.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Robust functional connectivity was observed between left and right dorsal (sensory) horns in healthy volunteers.
source: In a cohort of healthy volunteers, we observed robust functional connectivity between left and right ventral (motor) horns, and between left and right dorsal (sensory) horns.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Low-frequency BOLD fluctuations are inherent in the spinal cord as well as the brain.
source: Our results demonstrate that low-frequency BOLD fluctuations are inherent in the spinal cord as well as the brain, and by analogy to cortical circuits, we hypothesize that these correlations may offer insight into the execution and maintenance of sensory and motor functions both locally and within the cerebrum.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: These correlations may offer insight into the execution and maintenance of sensory and motor functions both locally and within the cerebrum.
source: Our results demonstrate that low-frequency BOLD fluctuations are inherent in the spinal cord as well as the brain, and by analogy to cortical circuits, we hypothesize that these correlations may offer insight into the execution and maintenance of sensory and motor functions both locally and within the cerebrum.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a hypothesis based on analogy to cortical circuits.

claim: The earliest fMRI papers investigated task-based fMRI, where evoked BOLD signal changes were interpreted as hemodynamic responses subsequent to neural activity.
source: The earliest papers investigated task-based fMRI, where evoked BOLD signal changes were interpreted as hemodynamic responses subsequent to neural activity (Ogawa et al., 1990; Bandettini et al., 1992; Kwong et al., 1992; Ogawa et al., 1992) and were used to infer which brain regions were activated for a specific task.
evidence: This is supported by citations to foundational fMRI papers.

claim: Biswal et al. established the existence of correlations between low-frequency (< 0.08 Hz) BOLD signals from spatially distinct locations when no task was performed in 1995.
source: The range and impact of fMRI methods were expanded in 1995 when Biswal et al. established the existence of correlations between low-frequency (< 0.08 Hz) BOLD signals from spatially distinct locations when no task was performed (Biswal et al., 1995), and over 4000 subsequent papers have documented different aspects of resting state fMRI.
evidence: This is supported by citation to the seminal Biswal et al. 1995 paper.

claim: Over 4000 papers have documented different aspects of resting state fMRI following the Biswal et al. 1995 study.
source: The range and impact of fMRI methods were expanded in 1995 when Biswal et al. established the existence of correlations between low-frequency (< 0.08 Hz) BOLD signals from spatially distinct locations when no task was performed (Biswal et al., 1995), and over 4000 subsequent papers have documented different aspects of resting state fMRI.
evidence: This is a statement about the volume of literature in the field.

claim: Resting state correlations have been widely adopted to infer functional connectivity between cortical regions.
source: Importantly, these correlations have been widely adopted to infer functional connectivity between cortical regions (Greicius et al., 2003; Fox et al., 2005; Smith, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to key papers in the field.

claim: fMRI in the spinal cord was first performed in 1996.
source: fMRI in the spinal cord was first performed (Yoshizawa et al., 1996) in 1996, and task-based (motor and/or sensory) spinal fMRI has since been demonstrated by a handful of groups worldwide (Stroman et al., 1999; Backes et al., 2001; Madi et al., 2001; Giove et al., 2004; Moffitt et al., 2005; Maieron et al., 2007; Giulietti et al., 2008; Agosta et al., 2009a; Cohen-Adad et al., 2010; Summers et al., 2010; Brooks et al., 2012; Sprenger et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yoshizawa et al., 1996.

claim: Task-based spinal fMRI has been demonstrated by a handful of groups worldwide.
source: fMRI in the spinal cord was first performed (Yoshizawa et al., 1996) in 1996, and task-based (motor and/or sensory) spinal fMRI has since been demonstrated by a handful of groups worldwide (Stroman et al., 1999; Backes et al., 2001; Madi et al., 2001; Giove et al., 2004; Moffitt et al., 2005; Maieron et al., 2007; Giulietti et al., 2008; Agosta et al., 2009a; Cohen-Adad et al., 2010; Summers et al., 2010; Brooks et al., 2012; Sprenger et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to spinal fMRI studies.

claim: Spinal cord fMRI has been shown to be sensitive to changes in patients with spinal cord injury.
source: Spinal cord fMRI has primarily been used to study motor and sensory/pain pathways in the healthy spinal cord, but has also been shown to be sensitive to changes in patients with spinal cord injury (Stroman et al., 2002, 2004; Kornelsen and Stroman, 2007) and multiple sclerosis (Agosta et al., 2008a, 2008b, 2009b; Valsasina et al., 2010, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies in spinal cord injury patients.

claim: Spinal cord fMRI has been shown to be sensitive to changes in patients with multiple sclerosis.
source: Spinal cord fMRI has primarily been used to study motor and sensory/pain pathways in the healthy spinal cord, but has also been shown to be sensitive to changes in patients with spinal cord injury (Stroman et al., 2002, 2004; Kornelsen and Stroman, 2007) and multiple sclerosis (Agosta et al., 2008a, 2008b, 2009b; Valsasina et al., 2010, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies in multiple sclerosis patients.

claim: Only one paper has reported an investigation of resting state BOLD fluctuations in the human spinal cord prior to this study, with equivocal results.
source: Importantly, these spinal fMRI studies were focused on understanding spinal cord function when performing tasks, and to date only one paper has reported an investigation of resting state BOLD fluctuations in the human spinal cord, from which the results were equivocal (Wei et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wei et al., 2010.

claim: The lack of positive reports of resting state spinal cord fMRI may reflect the relatively poor signal-to-noise ratio of spinal cord images achievable at conventional field strengths (1.5 Tesla and 3.0 Tesla).
source: Partly, the lack of positive reports may reflect the relatively poor signal-to-noise ratio of spinal cord images achievable at conventional field strengths (1.5 Tesla and 3.0 Tesla) and the inherent limitations of low spatial resolution in studying small structures.
evidence: This is an inference about why previous studies may have failed.

claim: Ultra-high magnetic fields (7 Tesla and above) provide new opportunities for high-resolution fMRI of the spinal cord with increased sensitivity to BOLD fluctuations.
source: The advent of ultra-high magnetic fields (7 Tesla and above) and implementation of appropriate multichannel spinal cord coils, along with improved image acquisition and correction protocols, provides new opportunities for high-resolution fMRI of the spinal cord with increased sensitivity to BOLD fluctuations in the small gray matter structures that are typically not well visualized at lower fields.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of the advantages of higher field strengths in MRI.

claim: The spinal cord is a long, cylindrical neural structure responsible for relaying motor and sensory information between the brain and body.
source: The spinal cord is essentially a long, cylindrical neural structure responsible for relaying motor and sensory information between the brain and body, it sits within a bath of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), and is surrounded by large vertebral bodies and intervertebral discs (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge, also illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The spinal cord sits within a bath of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and is surrounded by large vertebral bodies and intervertebral discs.
source: The spinal cord is essentially a long, cylindrical neural structure responsible for relaying motor and sensory information between the brain and body, it sits within a bath of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), and is surrounded by large vertebral bodies and intervertebral discs (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge, also illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: A butterfly-shaped gray matter structure surrounded by densely packed white matter is found within the spinal cord.
source: A butterfly-shaped gray matter structure surrounded by densely packed white matter is found within the cord (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge, also illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: The gray matter is anatomically described by ventral (anterior), lateral, and dorsal (posterior) horns.
source: The gray matter is anatomically described by ventral (anterior), lateral, and dorsal (posterior) horns, though the lateral and ventral horns in thoracic and lumbar segments are often summarized as anterior (ventrolateral) gray matter.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge.

claim: The dorsal horn contains neurons that receive sensory information from the extremities.
source: The dorsal horn contains neurons that receive sensory information from the extremities while upper motor neurons synapse onto lower motor neurons in the ventral horn, which relay information to the extremities (Kandel et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge supported by citation to Kandel et al., 2000.

claim: Upper motor neurons synapse onto lower motor neurons in the ventral horn, which relay information to the extremities.
source: The dorsal horn contains neurons that receive sensory information from the extremities while upper motor neurons synapse onto lower motor neurons in the ventral horn, which relay information to the extremities (Kandel et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge supported by citation to Kandel et al., 2000.

claim: Central pattern generators likely exist in the human spinal cord that subserve basic locomotion.
source: For example, the likely existence of central pattern generators in the human spinal cord that subserve basic locomotion (Kandel et al., 2000, p. 753) suggest that functional connectivity may exist between ventral (motor) horns.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kandel et al., 2000, p. 753.

claim: The existence of central pattern generators suggests that functional connectivity may exist between ventral (motor) horns.
source: For example, the likely existence of central pattern generators in the human spinal cord that subserve basic locomotion (Kandel et al., 2000, p. 753) suggest that functional connectivity may exist between ventral (motor) horns.
evidence: This is an inference based on known anatomy and function.

claim: Reflexes suggest connections between a dorsal (sensory) horn and both ipsilateral and contralateral ventral horns.
source: Similarly, reflexes suggest connections between a dorsal (sensory) horn and both ipsilateral and contralateral ventral horns (Kandel et al., 2000, Figure 36-2), and are primarily apparent in the presence of noxious stimuli.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kandel et al., 2000, Figure 36-2.

claim: Reflexes are primarily apparent in the presence of noxious stimuli.
source: Similarly, reflexes suggest connections between a dorsal (sensory) horn and both ipsilateral and contralateral ventral horns (Kandel et al., 2000, Figure 36-2), and are primarily apparent in the presence of noxious stimuli.
evidence: This is established physiological knowledge.

claim: The ascending sensory pathways and descending motor pathways suggest that there may be connectivity along the length of the cord.
source: The ascending sensory pathways and descending motor pathways also suggest that there may be connectivity along the length of the cord, at least within individual dermatomes for dorsal horns (Kandel et al., 2000, p. 445).
evidence: This is an inference based on known anatomy, supported by citation to Kandel et al., 2000, p. 445.

claim: The lack of a direct anatomical connection between two sub-regions of spinal gray matter does not preclude the possibility of finding connectivity between these regions because they may be indirectly connected via other pathways.
source: However, it must be emphasized that the lack of a direct anatomical connection between two sub-regions of spinal gray matter does not preclude the possibility of finding connectivity between these regions because they may be indirectly connected via other pathways.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the nature of functional connectivity.

claim: Functional images were preprocessed to mitigate rigid-body motion and physiological noise.
source: Functional images were preprocessed to mitigate rigid-body motion and physiological noise, and spatially interpolated to match the digital resolution of the T2*-weighted anatomical images (Figure 2).
evidence: This describes the preprocessing methods applied to the data.

claim: A 14-step standardized analysis protocol was used for each of the 22 subjects studied.
source: A 14-step standardized analysis protocol (described in 'Materials and methods') was used for each of the 22 subjects studied.
evidence: This describes the analysis methodology.

claim: A 30% increase in median TSNR (from 29.3 to 38.1) was observed across all 22 subjects after the application of CSF and white matter regressors.
source: Across all 22 subjects, we observed a 30% increase in median TSNR (from 29.3 to 38.1) after the application of these few regressors, demonstrating the importance of characterizing and removing structured noise sources (Xie et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data analysis.

claim: The increase in TSNR demonstrates the importance of characterizing and removing structured noise sources.
source: Across all 22 subjects, we observed a 30% increase in median TSNR (from 29.3 to 38.1) after the application of these few regressors, demonstrating the importance of characterizing and removing structured noise sources (Xie et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the TSNR improvement, supported by citation to Xie et al., 2012.

claim: Single-subject analyses show that statistically significant correlations are measurable between selected regions and are reproducible across subjects.
source: After band-pass filtering to isolate the frequency range of interest (0.01–0.08 Hz), single-subject analyses show that statistically significant correlations are measurable between selected regions and are reproducible across subjects.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from single-subject analyses.

claim: A seed region in the right ventral horn demonstrates connectivity with the contralateral ventral horns in the same slice and with adjacent slices.
source: As an illustrative example with the corresponding time series, an analysis performed on one subject (female, 23 years old) demonstrates connectivity with the contralateral ventral horns in the same slice and with adjacent slices when a seed region is selected in the center of the right ventral horn (Figure 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3 with data from a single subject.

claim: Gray matter correlations cannot be simply attributed to spatially correlated physiological noise and more likely represent genuine functional connectivity.
source: A stringent threshold of |z| > 3.29 (a two-tailed 99.9% confidence interval) was selected to show that connectivity is focused in the gray matter horns and not in central gray matter (connecting left and right sides and largely dominated by the central canal) nor adjacent white matter, which provides evidence that such gray matter correlations cannot be simply attributed to spatially correlated physiological noise and more likely represent genuine functional connectivity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the spatial specificity of the correlations.

claim: Reproducible focal connectivity is found between ventral horns in multiple subjects.
source: Further examples of within-slice connectivity analyses in single subjects confirm that reproducible focal connectivity is found between ventral horns (Figure 4A–F) and between dorsal horns (Figure 4G–J).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4A-F with data from multiple subjects.

claim: Reproducible focal connectivity is found between dorsal horns in multiple subjects.
source: Further examples of within-slice connectivity analyses in single subjects confirm that reproducible focal connectivity is found between ventral horns (Figure 4A–F) and between dorsal horns (Figure 4G–J).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4G-J with data from multiple subjects.

claim: There is evidence of plausible connectivity with central gray matter and between ventral and dorsal horns, but these correlations are less consistent across all slices and not statistically significant at the group level.
source: There is also evidence of plausible connectivity with central gray matter (Figure 4K) and between ventral and dorsal horns (Figure 4L), but these correlations are less consistent across all slices and not statistically significant at the group level.
evidence: This is based on single-subject analyses shown in Figure 4K and 4L, but lack of group-level significance.

claim: 67% of slices (177 of 264) exhibit significant correlations between ventral horns.
source: Across all 264 slices (12 slices/subject × 22 subjects), we observed that 67% of slices (177 of 264) exhibit significant correlations between ventral horns and 37% of slices (97 of 264) exhibit significant correlations between dorsal horns.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the group analysis.

claim: 37% of slices (97 of 264) exhibit significant correlations between dorsal horns.
source: Across all 264 slices (12 slices/subject × 22 subjects), we observed that 67% of slices (177 of 264) exhibit significant correlations between ventral horns and 37% of slices (97 of 264) exhibit significant correlations between dorsal horns.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the group analysis.

claim: Only about 20% of slices exhibited significant correlations between ventral and dorsal horn pairs.
source: In comparison, a markedly fewer number of slices (only 1 in 5) exhibited significant correlations between the remaining four pairs: 21% between left ventral and left dorsal horns (55 of 264), 21% between left ventral and right dorsal horns (55 of 264), 20% between right ventral and left dorsal horns (54 of 264), and 23% between right ventral and right dorsal horns (62 of 264).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the group analysis.

claim: Strong positive correlations are observed between left and right ventral horns at the group level (p < 0.01; corrected).
source: A group-level analysis of functional connectivity between sub-regions of spinal cord gray matter and adjacent white matter confirmed that the most robust correlations are observed between left and right ventral (motor) horns (p < 0.01; corrected), as well as between left and right dorsal (sensory) horns (p < 0.01; corrected) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the group-level statistical analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Strong positive correlations are observed between left and right dorsal horns at the group level (p < 0.01; corrected).
source: A group-level analysis of functional connectivity between sub-regions of spinal cord gray matter and adjacent white matter confirmed that the most robust correlations are observed between left and right ventral (motor) horns (p < 0.01; corrected), as well as between left and right dorsal (sensory) horns (p < 0.01; corrected) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the group-level statistical analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: No significant group-level correlations (p > 0.05) were observed between other gray matter sub-regions.
source: No significant group-level correlations (p > 0.05) were observed between other gray matter sub-regions, nor between spinal cord gray and white matter.
evidence: This is a result from the group-level statistical analysis.

claim: No significant group-level correlations were observed between spinal cord gray and white matter.
source: No significant group-level correlations (p > 0.05) were observed between other gray matter sub-regions, nor between spinal cord gray and white matter.
evidence: This is a result from the group-level statistical analysis.

claim: Weak positive correlations were observed between left and right dorsal column white matter (p < 0.05; corrected).
source: Weak positive correlations were observed between left and right dorsal column white matter (p < 0.05; corrected), and negative correlations were observed between left ventral white matter and right dorsal white matter (p < 0.01; corrected), and between right ventral white matter and both left (p < 0.01; corrected) and right (p < 0.01; corrected) dorsal white matter.
evidence: This is a result from the group-level statistical analysis.

claim: Negative correlations were observed between left ventral white matter and right dorsal white matter (p < 0.01; corrected).
source: Weak positive correlations were observed between left and right dorsal column white matter (p < 0.05; corrected), and negative correlations were observed between left ventral white matter and right dorsal white matter (p < 0.01; corrected), and between right ventral white matter and both left (p < 0.01; corrected) and right (p < 0.01; corrected) dorsal white matter.
evidence: This is a result from the group-level statistical analysis.

claim: Negative correlations were observed between right ventral white matter and both left and right dorsal white matter (p < 0.01; corrected).
source: Weak positive correlations were observed between left and right dorsal column white matter (p < 0.05; corrected), and negative correlations were observed between left ventral white matter and right dorsal white matter (p < 0.01; corrected), and between right ventral white matter and both left (p < 0.01; corrected) and right (p < 0.01; corrected) dorsal white matter.
evidence: This is a result from the group-level statistical analysis.

claim: The apparent existence of negative correlations in resting state spinal cord data is not unexpected because anticorrelations are commonly observed in resting state analyses of the brain.
source: The apparent existence of negative correlations in resting state spinal cord data is not unexpected because anticorrelations are commonly observed in resting state analyses of the brain (Chang and Glover, 2010) and have been a topic of intense discussion for over a decade.
evidence: This is an inference based on knowledge of brain resting state fMRI, supported by citation to Chang and Glover, 2010.

claim: The lower quartile is above zero in both gray matter plots, demonstrating that positive gray matter connectivity is a robust and reproducible measurement.
source: The lower quartile is above zero in both gray matter plots, demonstrating that positive gray matter connectivity is a robust and reproducible measurement.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the box-and-whisker plots in Figure 5B.

claim: Temporal correlations between white matter sub-regions are more variable and exhibit both positive and negative median correlations.
source: In comparison, temporal correlations between white matter sub-regions are more variable and exhibit both positive and negative median correlations.
evidence: This is an observation from the box-and-whisker plots in Figure 5B.

claim: Positive gray matter correlations are stable across various preprocessing procedures whereas white matter correlations are positive before but negative or non-significant after white matter regression.
source: Additional analyses were performed (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Figure 5—figure supplement 3, and Figure 5—figure supplement 5) to confirm that positive gray matter correlations are stable across various preprocessing procedures whereas white matter correlations are positive before but negative or non-significant after white matter regression (step #12).
evidence: This is a result from supplementary analyses shown in the figure supplements.

claim: Weaker positive correlations between sub-regions of left and right dorsal white matter remained positive and significant across various preprocessing configurations.
source: These supplementary analyses also showed that weaker positive correlations between sub-regions of left and right dorsal white matter remained positive and significant across various preprocessing configurations.
evidence: This is a result from supplementary analyses.

claim: This is the first conclusive demonstration that ultra-high field fMRI can non-invasively detect and characterize resting state BOLD signals within the gray matter of the human spinal cord.
source: We have presented the first conclusive demonstration that ultra-high field fMRI can non-invasively detect and characterize resting state BOLD signals within the gray matter of the human spinal cord.
evidence: This is a summary claim about the novelty of the study.

claim: Low-frequency temporal correlations were observed between gray matter horns in all subjects.
source: Low-frequency temporal correlations were observed between gray matter horns in all subjects, and examples of these correlations are presented in Figure 3 and Figure 4.
evidence: This is a summary of findings illustrated in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Within a given axial slice, the strongest and most robust correlations were between left and right ventral horns.
source: Within a given axial slice, the strongest and most robust correlations were between left and right ventral horns.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary finding.

claim: The reproducibility of correlations between ventral horns and between dorsal horns was demonstrated within a cohort of 22 healthy volunteers.
source: Correlations were also observed between left and right dorsal horns, and the reproducibility of correlations between ventral horns and between dorsal horns was demonstrated within a cohort of 22 healthy volunteers (Figure 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated in the group analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Correlations between ventral and dorsal gray matter were observed at the single-subject level but were less frequent and not statistically significant at the group level.
source: Although correlations between ventral and dorsal gray matter were also observed at the single-subject level (Figure 4L), such findings were less frequent and not statistically significant at the group level.
evidence: This is based on single-subject data in Figure 4L and group-level analysis.

claim: The absence of group-level correlations between spinal gray matter and adjacent white matter showed that these positive gray matter correlations are unlikely to be driven by spatially-correlated physiological noise.
source: The absence of group-level correlations between spinal gray matter and adjacent white matter showed that these positive gray matter correlations are unlikely to be driven by spatially-correlated physiological noise.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the pattern of correlations observed.

claim: Supplementary analyses without CSF or white matter regressors revealed strong correlations within gray matter and within white matter but not between gray and white matter.
source: In fact, supplementary analyses without CSF or white matter regressors (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a) revealed strong correlations within gray matter and within white matter but not between gray and white matter, suggesting that gray and white matter in the spinal cord may exhibit different degrees of physiological fluctuations.
evidence: This is a result from supplementary analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Gray and white matter in the spinal cord may exhibit different degrees of physiological fluctuations.
source: In fact, supplementary analyses without CSF or white matter regressors (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a) revealed strong correlations within gray matter and within white matter but not between gray and white matter, suggesting that gray and white matter in the spinal cord may exhibit different degrees of physiological fluctuations.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the supplementary analysis results.

claim: Additional analyses revealed that correlations within white matter were heavily influenced by preprocessing methodology.
source: The main analyses (Figure 5) also showed anticorrelations between white matter sub-regions. These observations were not unexpected because negative correlations are commonly seen in the brain (Chang and Glover, 2010), but additional analyses (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) revealed that correlations within white matter were heavily influenced by preprocessing methodology.
evidence: This is a result from supplementary analyses shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The nature of negative white matter correlations remains unclear and requires further investigation.
source: As a result, the nature of negative white matter correlations remains unclear and requires further investigation.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the current findings.

claim: Predominantly positive correlations between dorsal white matter sub-regions persisted across preprocessing permutations.
source: However, predominantly positive correlations between dorsal white matter sub-regions persisted across preprocessing permutations.
evidence: This is a result from supplementary analyses.

claim: Ding et al. recently reported the reliable detection of anisotropic correlations of resting state BOLD signals in brain white matter that appear to mimic white matter tracts identified by diffusion imaging methods.
source: Although the origins of these positive white matter correlations remain to be determined, and whereas in general BOLD signals from activation have been difficult to detect in brain white matter, we note that Ding et al. recently reported the reliable detection of anisotropic correlations of resting state BOLD signals in brain white matter that appear to mimic white matter tracts identified by diffusion imaging methods (Ding et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ding et al., 2013.

claim: Z-scores measured between ventral horns tended to be higher than z-scores measured between dorsal horns.
source: Another observation is that z-scores measured between ventral horns tended to be higher than z-scores measured between dorsal horns—a finding that was highly significant (p < 0.01 using a two-tailed Wilcoxon signed rank test; 'signrank' in Matlab).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from statistical analysis.

claim: The dorsal horns tend to be slightly narrower than the ventral horns, and thus may be more susceptible to registration inaccuracies, residual physiological noise, and partial volume averaging with adjacent white matter.
source: There are several possible reasons for this finding. Firstly, the dorsal horns tend to be slightly narrower than the ventral horns, and thus may be more susceptible to registration inaccuracies, residual physiological noise, and partial volume averaging with adjacent white matter.
evidence: This is an inference about potential sources of the observed difference.

claim: Signal dropout and unavoidable artifacts affect the dorsal horns but not ventral horns in a few slices, which would bias the results in favor of ventral horn connectivity.
source: Secondly, as shown in Figure 2, signal dropout and unavoidable artifacts affect the dorsal horns but not ventral horns in a few slices, which would bias the results in favor of ventral horn connectivity.
evidence: This is an observation from Figure 2 and an inference about its impact.

claim: Functional connectivity between dorsal horns may be more variable if the automated selection of gray matter sub-regions isolate signals from different laminae within dorsal horns.
source: Finally, even if spatial artifacts, registration inaccuracies, signal dropout, physiological noise, and partial volume averaging effects were minimized, it may be that functional connectivity between dorsal horns is more variable if the automated selection of gray matter sub-regions (step #14) isolate signals from different laminae within dorsal horns (Ruscheweyh and Sandkühler, 2002).
evidence: This is a speculation about a potential source of variability, supported by citation to Ruscheweyh and Sandkühler, 2002.

claim: Clinical applications of task-based spinal fMRI studies have primarily been targeted to subjects with multiple sclerosis and spinal cord injury.
source: To date, clinical applications of task-based spinal fMRI studies have primarily been targeted to subjects with multiple sclerosis (Agosta et al., 2008a, 2008b, 2009b; Valsasina et al., 2010, 2012) and spinal cord injury (SCI) (Stroman et al., 2002, 2004; Kornelsen and Stroman, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to relevant clinical studies.

claim: The non-invasive methods of resting state spinal cord functional connectivity may be most readily translatable to clinical investigations characterizing damage due to acute or chronic SCI and monitoring the efficacy of surgical or pharmacological interventions.
source: We propose that the non-invasive methods of resting state spinal cord functional connectivity developed in this paper may be most readily translatable to clinical investigations characterizing damage due to acute or chronic SCI and monitoring the efficacy of surgical or pharmacological interventions.
evidence: This is a proposal about potential clinical applications.

claim: Functional connectivity and the assessment of plasticity in the human spinal cord and animal models of SCI have been topics of intense research for many years.
source: Functional connectivity and the assessment of plasticity in the human spinal cord and animal models of SCI have been topics of intense research for many years (Bregman et al., 1997; Raineteau and Schwab, 2001; Cai et al., 2006; Freund et al., 2011) because SCI affects 260,000 people in the United States (a prevalence of ∼1 in 1200) with 11,000 new injuries reported each year (National Spinal Cord Injury Statistics Center, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to relevant research and statistics.

claim: SCI affects 260,000 people in the United States (a prevalence of ∼1 in 1200) with 11,000 new injuries reported each year.
source: Functional connectivity and the assessment of plasticity in the human spinal cord and animal models of SCI have been topics of intense research for many years (Bregman et al., 1997; Raineteau and Schwab, 2001; Cai et al., 2006; Freund et al., 2011) because SCI affects 260,000 people in the United States (a prevalence of ∼1 in 1200) with 11,000 new injuries reported each year (National Spinal Cord Injury Statistics Center, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to National Spinal Cord Injury Statistics Center, 2010.

claim: Studies have investigated the role of propriospinal neurons in partial recovery from incomplete SCI.
source: Studies have investigated the role of propriospinal neurons in partial recovery from incomplete SCI (Bareyre, 2008; Flynn et al., 2011a) while in vitro analyses of functional connectivity in mouse spinal cord have relied on electrophysiological methods (Flynn et al., 2011b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bareyre, 2008 and Flynn et al., 2011a.

claim: In vitro analyses of functional connectivity in mouse spinal cord have relied on electrophysiological methods.
source: Studies have investigated the role of propriospinal neurons in partial recovery from incomplete SCI (Bareyre, 2008; Flynn et al., 2011a) while in vitro analyses of functional connectivity in mouse spinal cord have relied on electrophysiological methods (Flynn et al., 2011b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Flynn et al., 2011b.

claim: A new intervention strategy using epidural stimulation and stand training has restored voluntary movement in four patients with complete paralysis.
source: A new intervention strategy using epidural stimulation and stand training was recently developed that has to date restored voluntary movement in four patients with complete paralysis, demonstrating that functional connectivity across a lesion may be restored with epidural stimulation (Angeli et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Angeli et al., 2014.

claim: Functional connectivity across a lesion may be restored with epidural stimulation.
source: A new intervention strategy using epidural stimulation and stand training was recently developed that has to date restored voluntary movement in four patients with complete paralysis, demonstrating that functional connectivity across a lesion may be restored with epidural stimulation (Angeli et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference from the results of Angeli et al., 2014.

claim: The majority of spinal injuries are incomplete, and lost function may eventually return to near-normal levels.
source: The majority of spinal injuries are, however, incomplete, and lost function may eventually return to near-normal levels; however, the progression of functional recovery after incomplete SCI remains poorly understood due to the absence of a non-invasive method to reliably assess spinal cord connectivity in vivo.
evidence: This is based on clinical knowledge about spinal cord injuries.

claim: The progression of functional recovery after incomplete SCI remains poorly understood due to the absence of a non-invasive method to reliably assess spinal cord connectivity in vivo.

claim: Resting state acquisitions of the cervical spinal cord will become a valuable tool for characterizing changes in functional connectivity in SCI.
source: We propose that resting state acquisitions of the cervical spinal cord will become a valuable tool for characterizing changes in functional connectivity in SCI, and for the prognosis and monitoring of progression of recovery via spontaneous repair and/or surgical intervention.
evidence: This is a proposal about future applications of the method.

claim: Observations of altered resting state connectivity in the brain in numerous disorders suggest that such correlations reflect an important level of organization and may play a fundamental role in the execution and maintenance of various functions.
source: Observations of altered resting state connectivity in the brain in numerous disorders (Fox and Greicius, 2010) and as a function of behavior or cognitive skills suggest that such correlations reflect an important level of organization and may play a fundamental role in the execution and maintenance of various functions (Pizoli et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fox and Greicius, 2010 and Pizoli et al., 2011.

claim: Investigation of resting state spinal cord networks could have widespread applicability in studying central nervous system diseases that affect motor and/or sensory pathways.
source: Thus, investigation of resting state spinal cord networks could similarly have widespread applicability in studying central nervous system diseases that affect motor and/or sensory pathways such as cervical spondylotic myelopathy, neuromyelitis optica, acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, arachnoiditis, transverse myelitis, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, and multiple sclerosis.
evidence: This is an inference about potential applications based on brain resting state fMRI findings.

claim: The study chose to constrain the group analysis to investigating connectivity within each axial slice rather than along the cord.
source: Firstly, although we observed statistically significant correlations along the cord in single-subject analyses (for example, in left ventral gray matter in Figure 3), we chose to constrain the group analysis to investigating connectivity within each axial slice.
evidence: This describes a methodological choice made in the study.

claim: Incorporating correlations along the cord would have made the analysis significantly more complicated by increasing the number of potential correlations by an order of magnitude.
source: This was done because incorporating correlations along the cord would have made the analysis significantly more complicated by increasing the number of potential correlations by an order of magnitude.
evidence: This is a justification for the methodological choice.

claim: Some slices exhibited regions of signal dropout at the dorsal edge caused by fat shift of the nerve root sleeve in the phase-encode direction.
source: Furthermore, as shown in Figure 2, some slices exhibited regions of signal dropout at the dorsal edge caused by fat shift of the nerve root sleeve in the phase-encode (anterior-posterior) direction.
evidence: This is an observation from Figure 2.

claim: The absence of a statistically significant correlation with a slice impacted by B0 inhomogeneities or an artifact cannot be interpreted as proof that connectivity does not exist between particular sub-regions of interest.
source: The absence of a statistically significant correlation with a slice impacted by main field (B0) inhomogeneities or an artifact cannot in and of itself be interpreted as proof that connectivity does not exist between particular sub-regions of interest, and ultimately very careful single-subject analyses will need to be performed to reliably characterize functional connectivity along the cord.
evidence: This is a statement about the interpretation of negative results.

claim: Further investigations of within-subject reproducibility still need to be performed.
source: Secondly, although we have investigated one aspect of reproducibility (via a group analysis of 22 healthy volunteers) and established the existence of spinal cord functional connectivity, further investigations of within-subject reproducibility still need to be performed.
evidence: This is a statement about future work needed.

claim: The reproducibility of these connectivity measures over months and years will need to be quantified before such techniques can be reliably used to study disease progression or gerontology.
source: The reproducibility of these connectivity measures over months and years will need to be quantified before such techniques can be reliably used to study disease progression or gerontology.
evidence: This is a statement about future work needed for clinical applications.

claim: This study reports empirical findings of functional connectivity in the spinal cord but does not directly address the physiological origins of these low-frequency BOLD signal fluctuations.
source: Thirdly, this study reports empirical findings of functional connectivity in the spinal cord but does not directly address the physiological origins of these low-frequency BOLD signal fluctuations.
evidence: This is a statement about the scope and limitations of the study.

claim: Observations of functional connectivity were first reported in the brain nearly two decades ago, and yet the origin of these fluctuations is still a topic of intense discussion.
source: However, as a point of reference, observations of functional connectivity were first reported in the brain nearly two decades ago (Biswal et al., 1995) and yet the origin of these fluctuations is still a topic of intense discussion.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Biswal et al., 1995 and knowledge of the field.

claim: Recent studies have combined tractography and functional imaging with techniques such as network analysis and graph theory to explore how resting state networks may have emerged.
source: Although the nature of resting state correlations is not fully understood, recent studies have combined tractography and functional imaging with techniques such as network analysis and graph theory to explore how these networks may have emerged (Deco et al., 2013a, 2013b; van den Heuvel and Sporns, 2013; Mišić et al., 2014; Goñi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies.

evidence: This is supported by citation to Buckner and Krienen, 2013.

claim: Low-frequency BOLD fluctuations in the brain and spinal cord may share the same origin.
source: We therefore propose that because the spinal cord is an integral part of the central nervous system, one simple explanation is that low-frequency BOLD fluctuations in the brain and spinal cord share the same origin.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: There may be long-range connections between networks in the spinal cord and cerebrum (and cerebellum).
source: This theory would then suggest that there may be long-range connections between networks in the spinal cord and cerebrum (and cerebellum), and future research should consider the nature of resting state networks not only within the brain but within the entire central nervous system.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the hypothesis about shared origins.

claim: At conventional field strengths (1.5 Tesla and 3.0 Tesla), the lower signal-to-noise ratio and BOLD contrast limit the spatial resolution and sensitivity for detecting BOLD signals.
source: At conventional field strengths (1.5 Tesla and 3.0 Tesla), the lower signal-to-noise ratio and BOLD contrast limit the spatial resolution and sensitivity for detecting BOLD signals, so large voxels are typically used and multiple acquisitions are averaged.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of MRI physics and practice.

claim: High resolution BOLD acquisitions of the spinal cord at 7 Tesla have not evolved as rapidly as for the brain in part due to the widespread dependence on single-shot echo-planar acquisitions at lower fields and the lack of specialized coils.
source: At 7 Tesla, high resolution BOLD acquisitions of the spinal cord have not evolved as rapidly as for the brain in part due to the widespread dependence on single-shot echo-planar acquisitions at lower fields and the lack of specialized coils to image the spinal cord.
evidence: This is an inference about the state of the field.

claim: These results are the first demonstrations of functional imaging of the human spinal cord at 7 Tesla.
source: Our results are the first demonstrations of functional imaging of the human spinal cord at 7 Tesla (Barry et al., 2013a) and high-resolution resting state functional connectivity in the spinal cord (Barry et al., 2013b), and are likely to be of significant relevance in understanding basic aspects of spinal cord function both in normal development and in clinical disorders of the central nervous system.
